strengths: The core intervention is simple, training-free, and practically appealing: dynamically reducing positional extrapolation during denoising can be added to PI, NTK-aware interpolation, and YaRN without extra sampling steps.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad. Results cover four high resolutions and two aspect ratios on FLUX, extrapolation from 256 to 320/384 on FiTv2, automatic metrics, qualitative crops, a human comparison, panorama generation, and scheduler ablations.

Reported improvements over the corresponding static baselines are generally consistent. The gains are especially substantial at 4096×4096, and the FiTv2 experiment suggests that the effect is not confined to one model or text-to-image generation.
The paper is visually clear and generally easy to follow. Comparisons with Lumina-Next help distinguish DYPE from the closest prior dynamic positional-encoding strategy.

The contribution is useful and moderately original: time-dependent positional extrapolation is not itself new, but transitioning toward the pretrained positional encoding and extending this principle systematically across several extrapolation schemes provides a distinct method.
weaknesses: The central soundness issue is that the spectral derivation does not establish the claimed behavior of reverse diffusion trajectories. Equations 10–12 analyze the marginal power spectrum of the forward mixture x_t=(1−t)x+tε. A change in an averaged marginal PSD does not show that individual Fourier components of a reverse-generated sample converge to their final values early, nor that those components subsequently cease evolving. The assumption connecting this calculation to positional-frequency allocation is stated but neither theoretically justified nor directly tested with reverse trajectories.

Most automatic metrics provide weak evidence for the central claim of improved ultra-high-frequency detail: CLIPScore, ImageReward, aesthetic predictors, and Inception-based FID resize images substantially. FID is additionally unreliable with only 195 Aesthetic-4K samples. No frequency-sensitive, patch-level, native-resolution, or reference reconstruction evaluation is reported.

Statistical reliability is insufficient. Results are presented without confidence intervals, multiple sampling seeds, significance tests, or seed-matching details. Scheduler choices are selected using 50 DrawBench prompts and then evaluated on the full DrawBench set, so the headline evaluation is not cleanly separated from hyperparameter selection.

The human-study protocol is under-specified: it is unclear how many comparisons each rater completed, whether presentation order and method identity were randomized or blinded, how ties were treated, and whether images were inspected at native resolution. The statement that 20 prompts were obtained by sampling every fourth entry from a 195-item dataset is also internally unclear. No uncertainty estimates are supplied despite preference rates being a major supporting result.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance in its current form. The project-page URL is blank, no code is supplied, and the manuscript omits random seeds, sampler and guidance settings, precise baseline implementations, metric versions and preprocessing, memory/runtime measurements, and sufficient human-study details. The limited implementation paragraph is not enough to reconstruct the experiments reliably.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. “State-of-the-art” and “unprecedented resolutions” are not supported by comprehensive comparisons; the FreeScale comparison changes both backbone and method, so it cannot isolate DYPE. “No inference overhead” is asserted without latency or memory measurements and appears to mean no additional denoising steps rather than literally zero overhead.

Presentation has correctable but meaningful inconsistencies. Equation 13 defines κ(t)=λ_s t^{λ_t}, so κ(0)=0, while the text says κ(0)=1; only the effective factor s^{κ(t)} becomes one. The paper also contains a placeholder citation (“YourTeam”), a blank project link, numerous grammatical errors, and some ambiguous terminology around image frequencies versus RoPE frequencies.

The paper provides no dedicated limitations or broader-impact discussion. In particular, it does not discuss failure modes outside the tested models, the substantial absolute compute/memory cost of full-attention 4K–6K generation, benchmark and aesthetic-model biases, or misuse risks of improved high-resolution synthesis. For the human study, recruitment, compensation, consent, and ethics-review status are not reported.

strengths: The method is simple and potentially useful: DYPE makes positional extrapolation time-dependent and can be applied to PI, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN without training or additional denoising steps.

The experiments report broadly consistent improvements over the corresponding static positional-encoding baselines. Table 1 covers several resolutions and aspect ratios on FLUX, while Table 3 provides some cross-model support using FiTv2 and ImageNet.

The advantage generally increases at the most challenging resolutions. The inclusion of automatic metrics, qualitative comparisons, a resolution-scaling study, and a human preference study is broader than relying on selected images alone.

The manuscript communicates the main intuition clearly and includes useful scheduler and implementation ablations. weaknesses: Soundness: the central spectral justification is not valid as presented. Equation 11 describes the marginal power spectrum of a forward mixture, not when semantic or frequency content in an actual reverse-model trajectory converges. Moreover, (1-t)^2 C/f^ω+t^2 is generally non-monotonic: its derivative vanishes at t=(C/f^ω)/(1+C/f^ω). This directly contradicts the asserted monotonicity used to define Equation 12, so the resulting quantity need not lie in [0,1] or demonstrate that low-frequency generated content has converged. The main mechanistic claim therefore lacks support even if the heuristic performs well.

The method description is internally inconsistent. For κ(t)=λ_s t^λ_t, κ(0)=0, not 1 as claimed. The equations recover no scaling because κ is used as an exponent or because YaRN thresholds collapse, but the text repeatedly describes κ itself as a scale tending to one. It is also unclear why λ_s should represent the resolution ratio when the equations already contain s; with λ_s=2, early DY-NTK scaling is effectively s squared.

The experiments establish correlation with one chosen schedule but do not validate the proposed mechanism. Important controls are missing, including a reversed schedule, a constant schedule with matched average scaling, abrupt early/late switching, and schedules derived quantitatively from the purported progression map. Without these, the gains could simply result from interpolation between two PE regimes rather than spectral convergence.

The evaluation lacks statistical reliability. No results across generation seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. FID computed from only 195 Aesthetic-4K pairs is particularly noisy, yet small FID differences are interpreted as meaningful. It is not stated how many samples per prompt were generated or whether seeds were paired across methods.

The claimed state-of-the-art fidelity is unsupported. The main comparisons are only against FLUX and static PE transformations. The FreeScale comparison changes both the method and backbone, so it cannot isolate algorithmic quality. Other training-free high-resolution methods discussed in related work are not evaluated under a common backbone, compute budget, or protocol.

The human study is insufficiently documented: the manuscript does not report the number of judgments per condition, rater recruitment, compensation, exclusions, randomization, side swapping, blinding, agreement, uncertainty, or consent/ethics procedures. The unusually large 87–90% preferences therefore cannot be independently assessed.

Reproducibility is poor. The project-page field is blank, no code is supplied, and the references contain a literal placeholder citation. Essential details such as the exact definition of context length and per-axis s, random seeds, sampler and guidance settings, VAE and precision configuration, metric implementations and preprocessing, attention-scaling handling, and memory strategy for 4K–6K generation are missing.

Originality is limited because Lumina-Next already introduced time-aware positional scaling in a DiT. DYPE uses a different trajectory toward unscaled RoPE and generalizes the wrapper to several extrapolation schemes, but this is an incremental distinction whose claimed principled derivation is undermined by the spectral-analysis error.

Several claims are overstated or ambiguous. “No inference overhead” ignores the very large cost of processing the longer token sequence and is defensible only relative to another method generating at the same target resolution. “Unprecedented resolutions” and “true end-to-end” are not substantiated by comprehensive comparisons or runtime and memory measurements.

Limitations and ethics receive inadequate treatment. The conclusion offers future work but does not discuss failure modes, dependence on FLUX/FiTv2 and RoPE, metric limitations, prompt or demographic biases, compute and environmental costs, or potential misuse of high-resolution generation. No material model-specific safety analysis is provided, and the human-subject procedure lacks an ethics statement.

Presentation contains numerous technical and editorial defects beyond ordinary typos, including the κ endpoint contradiction, inconsistent descriptions of YaRN bands, malformed or placeholder references, an empty project link, and selective qualitative figures whose small crops do not permit rigorous verification of 4K detail. Overall, promising empirical observations do not overcome the unsupported central explanation and insufficiently reproducible evaluation.

strengths: The core idea is simple, original, and practically useful: making RoPE extrapolation depend on the denoising timestep requires no retraining or extra sampling steps and can be layered onto existing position-extrapolation methods.

The empirical scope is broader than is typical for an inference-time modification. Results cover FLUX text-to-image generation on DrawBench and Aesthetic-4K, FiTv2 class-conditional generation on 50,000 ImageNet samples, multiple aspect ratios, and resolutions up to 6144×6144.

The reported gains are generally consistent. In particular, at 4096×4096 DY-YaRN substantially improves over YaRN on DrawBench and Aesthetic-4K, while its advantage also appears in the human evaluation, resolution-scaling study, and FiTv2 experiments.

Ablations compare scheduler forms, parameter choices, and three ways of injecting timestep dependence into YaRN. The comparison with Lumina-Next's time-aware RoPE helps distinguish DYPE from the closest conceptual precedent.

The manuscript is clearly organized and its qualitative figures make the failure modes and fine-detail improvements easy to understand. The contribution is significant for inexpensive resolution extrapolation in diffusion transformers.
weaknesses: The proposed spectral justification is not fully sound. Equations 10–12 characterize the marginal power spectrum of the analytically constructed noisy mixture x_t=(1-t)x+tε; they do not establish that individual Fourier coefficients along a learned reverse-generation trajectory converge to their final values at different times. The key step from marginal PSD evolution to which positional frequencies the denoiser needs is explicitly introduced as an assumption and is not directly validated with trajectory- or attention-level measurements.

Equation 13 contains a material inconsistency: κ(t)=λ_s t^{λ_t} gives κ(0)=0, whereas the text states κ(0)=1. Later sections rely on the former behavior to recover unscaled RoPE. The implementation section also says λ_s=λ_t=2 for all experiments, while DY-YaRN is defined with λ_s=1. These errors leave the exact method insufficiently specified.

The strongest state-of-the-art and unprecedented-resolution claims are not supported by a sufficiently controlled comparison. Most baselines are only FLUX with static positional scaling; FreeScale is compared using a different, older backbone, and other contemporary high-resolution methods are not evaluated on a shared base model and protocol.

Uncertainty is not reported. Aesthetic-4K contains only 195 pairs, making its FID estimate potentially unstable, and no multiple-seed statistics or confidence intervals are given. The scheduler was selected on 50 DrawBench prompts, but it is unclear whether this subset is separated from subsequent evaluation, so some reported results may reflect hyperparameter-selection bias.

The human study reports striking 87–90% preferences but omits essential protocol details such as image/randomization procedure, whether raters evaluated all comparisons, tie handling, inter-rater agreement, participant recruitment and compensation, and statistical uncertainty.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for an acceptance-level release: the project-page field is blank, no code is supplied, important engineering details needed to reproduce 4K–6K FLUX inference on one L40S are absent, and runtime, memory use, attention implementation, random seeds, and exact generation settings are not reported. A placeholder citation also remains in the bibliography.

The paper lacks a limitations and broader-impact discussion. It does not address dependence on RoPE-based DiTs, degradation beyond the tested range, the substantial compute still required for quadratic attention, inherited model biases and image-generation misuse, or ethics/consent considerations for the 50-person study. These issues reduce confidence and reach but do not negate the empirical contribution.

strengths: The core method is simple, training-free, and practically useful: timestep-dependent variants of PI, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN can be added to pretrained diffusion transformers without extra denoising steps or fine-tuning.

The empirical study is broad. It includes FLUX and FiTv2 in the main experiments, additional Qwen-Image and Wan results, resolutions up to 6144×6144, multiple aspect ratios, automatic metrics, qualitative comparisons, ablations, and a 50-rater preference study.

The strongest results occur in the intended ultra-high-resolution regime. For example, at 4096×4096 on DrawBench, DY-YaRN substantially improves over YaRN in CLIPScore (26.94 vs. 25.71), ImageReward (0.15 vs. -0.34), and aesthetics (5.17 vs. 4.85); it also obtains roughly 87–90% human preference over YaRN across the three criteria.

The comparison with TASR/Lumina-Next helps distinguish the contribution from prior timestep-aware positional scaling: DYPE moves toward the pretrained, unscaled encoding late in denoising rather than retaining interpolation that may suppress high-frequency detail.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually communicates the observed failure modes and improvements. The contribution is significant for extending existing DiTs, although its originality is moderate because timestep-dependent RoPE scaling already exists and the main novelty is the direction and schedule of that transition.
weaknesses: The proposed theoretical motivation is not sufficiently established. Equations 10–12 describe the ensemble power spectrum of the forward mixture distribution, not convergence of individual semantic Fourier components along an actual learned reverse trajectory. Power alone also discards phase. Thus the assertion that low-frequency content has 'converged' and no longer needs corresponding positional frequencies does not directly follow; a frequency-wise error-to-final-sample analysis or causal intervention would be needed.

There is a material mathematical inconsistency in the method definition. Equation 13 gives κ(t)=λ_s t^{λ_t}, so κ(0)=0, whereas the text explicitly states κ(0)=1. The formulas obtain no scaling because κ becomes an exponent or collapses YaRN's thresholds, but the incorrect explanation makes the precise algorithm ambiguous. The roles of λ_s, the resolution ratio s, and the different DY-YaRN schedule are also described inconsistently.

Statistical support is weak. No confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or significance tests are reported, despite many modest gains over static YaRN. FID is reported on only 195 Aesthetic-4K pairs, where it is likely noisy, and the protocol and sample counts underlying the cross-method FID/patch-FID/IS comparison in Table 3 are not adequately specified.

Several baseline comparisons are difficult to interpret fairly. Table 3 mixes methods using different pretrained backbones, tuning, super-resolution, and progressive pipelines without controlling compute or model capacity. The additional Qwen, video, editing, and panorama studies are promising but use small or unspecified samples and provide little implementation detail.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted version. Code is only promised after acceptance, while essential details such as seeds, noise matching, sampler and guidance settings, memory/precision strategy, metric implementations, patch extraction, preprocessing, and exact sample counts are missing. The claim that all experiments—including 4096–6144-square FLUX generation—run on one L40S particularly requires a detailed memory and runtime account.

The claim of 'no additional sampling cost' needs qualification: DYPE may add negligible overhead relative to generating at the same resolution, but full-attention inference itself grows sharply with resolution. Runtime, peak memory, and comparisons against progressive or super-resolution pipelines are absent.

The human study lacks information about recruitment, consent, compensation, demographics, blinding, order randomization, ties, and aggregation. More seriously, the Impact Statement claims that the research 'does not involve human subjects,' directly contradicting the reported study with 50 raters. The limitations discussion is also largely absent and does not acknowledge metric reliability, baseline comparability, computational scaling, or possible model-specific tuning.

strengths: The paper studies a practical and important problem: extending pretrained diffusion transformers to substantially higher spatial resolutions through a lightweight, training-free positional-encoding modification. The empirical evaluation is broad. It covers FLUX and FiTv2 in the main paper, adds Qwen-Image and Wan2.1 in the appendix, examines several resolutions and aspect ratios, and reports automatic, qualitative, and human evaluations. Tables 1 and 4 generally show improvements over the corresponding static positional-extrapolation baselines.

The comparison against TASR is relevant because TASR is also time-dependent, and the scheduler/application ablations in Tables 6 and 7 provide some evidence that the particular direction and location of the dynamic adjustment matter.
The high-level motivation and implementation are reasonably easy to understand, and the qualitative examples show visible reductions in repetition and structural artifacts at extreme resolutions.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central spectral argument does not establish the claimed mechanism. Equation 11 describes the marginal power spectrum of an analytically forward-noised mixture; it does not show that individual Fourier components of a reverse-sampling trajectory have converged or ceased changing. More seriously, (1-t)^2 C/f^omega + t^2 is generally non-monotone in t: its derivative vanishes at t=(C/f^omega)/(1+C/f^omega). Therefore the monotonicity assumed immediately before Equation 12 is false, and the resulting normalized progression index need not lie in [0,1]. The paper also assumes, without analysis or intervention, that image Fourier frequencies correspond to RoPE frequency bands in the manner needed to justify the proposed allocation. This leaves the main explanatory claim unsupported even if the heuristic performs well.

The method specification contains important inconsistencies. Equation 13 defines kappa(t)=lambda_s t^lambda_t, so kappa(0)=0, while the text explicitly states kappa(0)=1. The later equations achieve no scaling through an exponent of zero or collapsed YaRN thresholds, but that is different from the stated unifying argument. Moreover, lambda_s is described as reflecting the target/training context ratio, yet the implementation fixes lambda_s=2 across different extrapolation ratios. The paper does not isolate whether the gains come from the proposed spectral principle, a favorable generic annealing schedule, attention-logit scaling, or hyperparameter tuning.

The quantitative evidence lacks statistical reliability. No results include variability across seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. DrawBench contains only 200 prompts and Aesthetic-4K only 195 pairs, making FID particularly unstable at the apparent sample count. Patch-FID and patch-IS are not defined sufficiently, including crop sampling and effective sample size. The resolution-scaling study uses only 20 prompts, and the attention-entropy advantage over YaRN is extremely small (MAE 0.0455 versus 0.0476) without uncertainty. Claims such as state-of-the-art fidelity and increasingly pronounced gains are consequently stronger than the evidence supports.

The general-baseline comparison in Table 3 is difficult to interpret fairly. It mixes different backbone models, tuned systems, progressive pipelines, super-resolution, and combinations with HiFlow, but does not provide enough information about baseline configurations, sampling budgets, prompt/seed matching, or whether every baseline was rerun under an identical protocol. Global FID/IS on this small prompt-conditioned benchmark also does not directly demonstrate faithful ultra-high-resolution detail.

The human evaluation is inadequately documented. Although 50 raters are mentioned, the paper omits the number of judgments per comparison, rater assignment, recruitment and compensation, display hardware or zoom protocol for judging 4096-square images, side randomization, ties, agreement, uncertainty, and consent/approval procedures. The Impact Statement incorrectly says the research does not involve human subjects despite this study. This is a material ethics and reporting issue, not a penalty for honestly discussing limitations.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Code is only promised after acceptance, and essential details are absent: random seeds, guidance and sampler settings, target-resolution scaling calculations in token rather than pixel coordinates, metric implementations and preprocessing, baseline hyperparameters, patch extraction, prompt-to-seed policy, and complete human-study materials. The appendix gives GPU type, step count, and a few PE parameters, but not enough to reproduce the principal tables.

Originality is moderate rather than high: dynamically varying positional extrapolation during denoising already appears in TASR/Lumina-Next. DYPE proposes a different schedule direction and demonstrates useful empirical behavior, but the claimed principled derivation is flawed. Presentation is also weakened by overclaims, equation/prose contradictions, numerous editing errors, and the absence of a candid limitations section. Overall, the promising heuristic and broad experiments do not overcome the central soundness and evaluation deficiencies.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical evidence is broad and mostly consistent. The paper includes useful ablations of scheduler form, magnitude, and where timestep conditioning is applied. Comparisons against static RoPE extensions and the related time-aware TASR baseline help isolate the proposed mechanism.

Significance: A training-free modification that substantially improves 3K–4K generation, requires no extra denoising steps, and can be layered onto existing DiTs is practically useful. The advantage generally increases with extrapolation distance, which matches the intended use case.

Originality: Dynamically moving the positional-frequency allocation toward unscaled RoPE is a simple but insightful extension of existing PI, NTK-aware, and YaRN methods. Applying the idea across text-to-image, class-conditional generation, video, editing, and panoramic synthesis suggests useful generality.

Presentation: The main idea and implementation are easy to understand, and the many qualitative examples, zoomed comparisons, human preferences, scaling study, and attention-entropy analysis provide complementary views of performance.
weaknesses: The theoretical motivation is not fully sound as written. Equation 11 characterizes marginals of the forward corruption process, not the evolution or convergence of Fourier modes along a model-generated reverse trajectory. Thus it does not by itself establish the central claim that particular modes in a generated sample have already converged and no longer require positional capacity.

Several mathematical statements are internally inconsistent. With κ(t)=λ_s t^{λ_t}, κ(0)=0, not 1 as stated. Likewise, Equation 12 gives γ(f,0)=0 and γ(f,1)=1, whereas the Figure 2 caption describes saturation near t≈0 in the opposite orientation. These errors obscure the claimed connection between the analysis and scheduler design.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated seeds, and significance tests. FID computed from only 195 Aesthetic-4K pairs is especially noisy, while many ablations and extensions use only 20–50 prompts. The large human-preference margins are encouraging, but the paper omits assignment counts, randomization/blinding, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty intervals.

The comparison to general high-resolution systems mixes different backbones and procedures, with insufficient information about whether all baselines were rerun using identical prompts, seeds, and metric implementations. Consequently, the broad state-of-the-art claim is less convincing than the controlled comparisons against static positional-encoding baselines.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: code is promised only upon acceptance, and the implementation section provides very few details beyond α, β, step count, GPU, and λ values. Exact model revisions, sampler and guidance settings, seeds, preprocessing, metric configurations, attention scaling, and baseline configurations are missing.

The statement that the method has “no additional sampling cost” needs qualification: it may add negligible overhead relative to generating at the same target resolution, but ultra-high-resolution self-attention itself is dramatically more expensive than native-resolution inference.

Research-ethics reporting is inconsistent. The impact statement says the work does not involve human subjects, yet Section 4.1 reports a study with 50 human raters. Recruitment, consent, compensation, privacy, and applicable ethics-review or exemption information should be provided.

Presentation has avoidable issues, including grammatical errors, duplicated or placeholder-like appendix prose, and dense tables. Overall, this is a promising and practically useful contribution, but the theoretical inconsistencies and incomplete experimental reporting keep it at weak accept rather than accept.
